title: Oregon
subtitle: Pinot Noir in the north-west
objectives: Explain why Pinot Noir suits Oregon
Explain Oregon's labelling and farming culture

steps.title: Willamette Valley
steps.body: Oregon's wine centre is the Willamette Valley, south of Portland, at about 45 degrees north, the same latitude as Burgundy. The climate is cool and maritime, with wet winters and dry summers. David Lett planted Pinot Noir there in 1965, and his 1975 wine did well against Burgundy in a 1979 Paris tasting.

steps.title: Pinot's natural home
steps.body: Pinot Noir is over 60% of Oregon's plantings. The cool climate keeps acidity and red fruit, and long, dry autumns ripen it slowly. Volcanic Jory soil in the Dundee Hills and marine sediments in places like Yamhill-Carlton give different styles. Pinot Gris and, increasingly, Chardonnay are the main whites.

steps.prompt: Why does Pinot Noir thrive in the Willamette Valley?
options: A cool climate and long, dry autumns
steps.explanation: Cool conditions keep acidity and fruit purity, while dry autumns let grapes ripen slowly.

steps.title: A small-producer culture
steps.body: Oregon wineries are mostly small and family-run. The state requires 90% of a named grape on the label, stricter than federal rules. Sustainable, organic and biodynamic farming are widespread. Burgundian houses like Maison Joseph Drouhin invested from 1987, a sign of respect for the region.

steps.prompt: Match each Oregon feature to its detail.
steps.explanation: Oregon's history is short but focused.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The Willamette Valley lies at Burgundy's latitude
Pinot Noir is over 60% of plantings
Oregon is mostly small producers, with strict labelling
